Introduction to SQL: SQL is a language for retrieving and managing information in relational databases. Businesses use it to answer questions from stored data.
Setting Up Your Environment: Prepare the database software and tools needed to write queries and inspect results.
Querying Data with SELECT: Retrieve chosen columns and rows from database tables for analysis and reporting.
DDL Commands: Define and change database structures, including tables and their rules.
DML Commands: Add, change, or remove stored records while keeping data consistent.
Filtering Data: Select records that meet specific conditions so reports focus on relevant information.
SQL Joins Basics: Combine related tables through matching fields to bring separate information together.
Advanced SQL Joins: Handle more complex table relationships, unmatched records, and repeated matches accurately.
Set Operators: Combine or compare query results to identify shared, distinct, or additional records.
SQL Functions Overview: Use built-in operations to transform values and calculate useful results within queries.
String Functions: Clean and reshape text fields to improve consistency in business records.
Numeric Functions: Perform calculations and adjust numeric values for reporting and analysis.
Date and Time Functions: Work with dates, durations, and reporting periods to analyze activity over time.
NULL Functions: Handle missing or unknown values explicitly so calculations and reports remain meaningful.
CASE Statements: Apply conditional rules to classify records or calculate values within a query.
Aggregate Functions: Summarize multiple records into totals, counts, averages, and other business measures.
Window Functions Basics: Calculate across related rows while keeping each individual record visible.
Window Aggregate Functions: Compute running totals and group summaries without collapsing the underlying records.
Window Ranking Functions: Assign positions within a dataset to support comparisons and prioritization.
Window Value Functions: Compare values from nearby rows or find the first and last values within a group.
Advanced SQL Techniques: Organize complex queries into clearer, reusable steps for demanding data tasks.
Subqueries: Use the result of one query inside another to resolve multi-step data questions.
Common Table Expressions: Name temporary query results to make complex SQL easier to read and maintain.
Views: Save a query as a reusable database object that presents a consistent view of data.
CTAS and Temporary Tables: Store query results in new or temporary tables for staged processing. Available syntax depends on the database platform.
Comparing Advanced SQL Techniques: Choose between query structures based on readability, reuse, and measured performance.
Stored Procedures: Package database operations into reusable routines for consistent processing.
Triggers: Run database logic automatically when specified data changes occur.
Indexes: Create lookup structures that can speed up reads, with storage and write-performance tradeoffs.
Execution Plans: Inspect how the database processes a query to identify expensive operations.
Partitions: Divide large datasets into manageable sections to support maintenance and selected access patterns.
SQL Performance Optimization Tips: Measure query behavior and improve access patterns, joins, and processing efficiency.
AI and SQL: Use AI assistance to draft and explain SQL, while checking correctness and protecting sensitive information.
SQL Data Warehouse: Build a central analytical data store that combines sources for consistent reporting.
Data Warehouse Bronze Layer: Preserve incoming source data with minimal changes so it can be traced and reprocessed.
Data Warehouse Silver Layer: Clean and standardize source records into more reliable data for downstream use.
Data Warehouse Gold Layer: Create business-focused tables and measures ready for dashboards and analysis.
Exploratory Data Analysis: Examine patterns, unusual values, and data quality before drawing conclusions.
Advanced Data Analytics: Use deeper SQL analysis to investigate trends, segments, and business performance.
What Is Python and How It Works: Understand how Python executes instructions and supports automation, analysis, and software development.
Installing Python: Set up Python and the tools needed to run and manage programs.
Comments and print(): Document the purpose of code and display information to understand program behavior.
Variables: Store named values that a program can use and update during execution.
User input(): Accept information from a person while a program runs and prepare it for processing.
Python Data Types: Understand how Python represents text, numbers, collections, and other kinds of values.
String Basics and Transformations: Work with text and reshape it for cleaning, processing, and presentation.
Indexing and Slicing: Access individual items or selected portions of text and other sequences.
Search, Validation, and Case Conversion: Find text, check its format, and standardize letter casing for consistent records.
Integers and Floats, Numeric Types, and: Work with whole and decimal numbers and perform numerical calculations.
Rounding, Random Numbers, and Numeric Va: Control numerical precision, generate randomized values, and check whether inputs meet numeric requirements.
Boolean Values: Represent true-or-false states used in decisions and validation.
Comparison and Logical Operators: Compare values and combine conditions to express decision rules.
Membership and Identity Operators: Check whether a value belongs to a collection or whether references point to the same object.
If, Else, and Elif: Choose which instructions to run based on whether conditions are satisfied.
Nested and Advanced Conditions: Combine multiple decisions to handle more complex rules and situations.
Inline If and Match Case: Express simple choices compactly or select behavior by matching structured cases.
For Loops: Repeat processing across a collection of items to automate recurring tasks.
Break, Continue, and Pass: Control loop execution by stopping, skipping an iteration, or leaving a placeholder.
For Else and Nested Loops: Handle completion without an early break and repeat operations across multiple levels of data.
While Loops: Repeat instructions while a condition remains true, with clear stopping rules.
Lists Overview: Understand ordered, changeable collections used to manage groups of values.
Creating and Accessing Lists: Build lists and retrieve their items for further processing.
Unpacking and Analyzing Lists: Separate list contents into variables and examine their size or structure.
Adding, Removing, and Updating Items: Maintain a collection by inserting, deleting, or changing its contents.
Sorting and Combining Lists: Arrange items in a useful order and bring separate collections together.
Iterables and Filtering: Process values one at a time and retain only those that meet chosen conditions.
Lambda Expressions and List Comprehensio: Write compact transformations and filtering operations while preserving readability.
Tuples: Store ordered collections whose structure should remain unchanged.
Sets: Manage unique values and compare overlaps or differences between collections.
Dictionaries: Organize information as key-value pairs for clear, efficient lookup.
Functions Introduction: Group related instructions into reusable units that perform a defined task.
Function Parameters and Return Values: Pass information into functions and receive results for use elsewhere.
Types of Python Functions: Distinguish built-in functions, custom functions, and common function forms.
Writing Clean Functions: Design focused, readable functions that are easier to test, reuse, and maintain.
